---
title: "Assessing predictions and simulations"
description: >
  Comparing models by spatial cross-validation, and assessing prediction
  targets on data simulated from a known model.
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 6.5,
  fig.height = 4.5,
  out.width = "85%",
  fig.align = "center",
  dpi = 150
)
options(RiskMap.messages = FALSE)
# The simulation study refits two models to 50 simulated datasets, which takes
# a few minutes, so precompute.R runs it once, with the code shown below, and
# the article loads the result. The boundaries are downloaded there too.
boundaries <- readRDS("precomputed/liberia-boundaries.rds")
precomputed <- readRDS("precomputed/assessing-predictions.rds")
```

Whether a model predicts well can be judged in two ways. Cross-validation
predicts held-out data from the rest and scores the predictions against what
was observed. A simulation study generates data from a known model, so the
predictions can be scored against the true surface, at locations and over
areas, for the targets that matter. This article does both.

## Two models

The models are binomial models of river blindness in 90 Liberian villages, one
with only a spatial Gaussian process and one that adds the logarithm of
elevation.

```{r fit-models, message = FALSE}
library(RiskMap)
library(sf)

data(liberia)
liberia <- st_as_sf(liberia,
                    coords = c("long", "lat"),
                    crs = 4326)
crs <- propose_crs(liberia, messages = FALSE)
liberia <- st_transform(liberia, crs)

set.seed(2026)
fit_spatial <- glgpm(npos ~ gp(),
                     data = liberia,
                     family = "binomial",
                     denominator = ntest)
fit_elevation <- glgpm(npos ~ log_elevation + gp(),
                       data = liberia,
                       family = "binomial",
                       denominator = ntest)
```

## Spatial cross-validation

`assess_prediction()` splits the villages into test sets, predicts each test
set from the other villages and scores the predictions. With
`method = "cluster"` the test sets are spatial clusters, so that a test village
is not predicted from close neighbours alone. The two models have different
numbers of parameters, so `keep_par_fixed = FALSE` refits each to every
training set. Fixing the parameters at the estimates from all the data is
faster, but lets the test data inform the parameters.

```{r cross-validation}
cv <- assess_prediction(list(spatial = fit_spatial,
                             elevation = fit_elevation),
                        method = "cluster",
                        fold = 5,
                        keep_par_fixed = FALSE,
                        seed = 1)
cv
```

When a refit warns that the check for other maxima of the likelihood found a
higher maximum than the one reached from the starting values, the check has
done its job, and the refit takes the higher maximum.

The continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) compares the whole predictive
distribution with the observed count, and its scaled version (SCRPS) weighs
villages whose predictions have very different spreads more evenly. Lower is
better for both. The PIT area
measures how far the predictions are from calibration, and is compared with
its value for a perfectly calibrated model on the same test data. `summary()`
gives the scores of each test set, and `to_table()` formats them for a report.

```{r cross-validation-table}
to_table(cv)
```

`plot()` maps the scores at the test villages and draws the calibration curve,
and `plot_cross_validation()` chooses one of them.

```{r cross-validation-pit}
plot_cross_validation(cv, metric = "PIT")
```

A curve close to the diagonal means calibrated predictions, with observed
counts as likely to fall in each part of the predictive distribution as the
predictions say.

## A simulation study

Cross-validation scores predictions of the data. Decisions often rest on
other targets, such as the prevalence of an area or whether it exceeds a
threshold, which are never observed. A simulation study scores those. It
starts from a model with known parameters, here those estimated from the
Liberian data, specified with `specify_glgpm()`.

```{r specify-model}
truth <- specify_glgpm(npos ~ gp(),
                       data = liberia,
                       family = "binomial",
                       denominator = ntest,
                       parameters = coef(fit_spatial))
truth
```

```{r load-boundaries, include = FALSE}
border <- boundaries$border
counties <- boundaries$counties
```

`simulate_glgpm()` simulates the surface on a grid together with data at the
villages. `plot()` maps a simulated surface.

```{r simulate}
grid <- create_grid(border, spacing = 5)
simulations <- simulate_glgpm(truth,
                              nsim = 50,
                              what = c("data", "surface"),
                              prediction_grid = grid,
                              seed = 1)
plot(simulations)
```

`assess_simulation()` refits each candidate model to every simulated dataset,
predicts the surface, and scores the predictions against the truth. The
candidates here differ in the smoothness of the spatial process, the
exponential correlation of the generating model against a smoother Matérn
correlation with $\kappa = 1.5$. The predictions are scored at the grid points
and over the counties, by their mean squared error and by how well they
classify prevalence into the classes below 10%, 10% to 20% and above 20%.

```{r candidates}
fit_smooth <- glgpm(npos ~ gp(kappa = 1.5),
                    data = liberia,
                    family = "binomial",
                    denominator = ntest)
```

```{r assess-simulation, eval = FALSE}
assessment <- assess_simulation(simulations,
                                models = list(exponential = fit_spatial,
                                              smooth = fit_smooth),
                                spatial_scale = c("location", "area"),
                                aggregate = "mean",
                                boundaries = counties,
                                label = "shapeName",
                                objective = c("mse", "classify"),
                                breaks = c(0, 0.1, 0.2, 1),
                                seed = 1)
```

```{r assess-load, include = FALSE}
assessment <- precomputed$assessment
```

```{r assessment-print}
assessment
```

`summary()` gives each score with its spread over the simulations, and the
sensitivity, specificity and predictive values of each class.

```{r assessment-summary}
summary(assessment)
```

Here the two correlations predict almost equally well, at the grid points and
over the counties, so for these targets the choice of smoothness matters
little.

Fifty simulations give a first answer. A study meant to settle a choice needs
more, and the spread of the scores over the simulations shows how many.

## Learn more

Chapter [4](https://www.mbgr.org/04_geostatistical-prediction.html) of the book
*Model-based geostatistics for global public health using R* treats the
assessment of predictive performance, by cross-validation and by simulation.
